title: The Money Printer and the Emperor

preview: The Federal Reserve has printed roughly three trillion dollars since March. The Reserve Bank of Australia has launched its first quantitative easin...
content:
The Federal Reserve has printed roughly three trillion dollars since March. The Reserve Bank of Australia has launched its first quantitative easing program in history. The European Central Bank has expanded bond-buying by another seven hundred and fifty billion euros. The Bank of Japan, already printing for decades, has accelerated.

The numbers are too large to comprehend, which I suspect is part of why they generate less alarm than they should. A trillion dollars has no referent in human experience. You can't picture it or feel it. The number is an abstraction stacked on an abstraction, and the mind slides off it like water off glass.

So let me make it concrete. The United States government is spending money it doesn't have, in quantities it has never spent before, and funding that spending by creating new money. The Treasury issues bonds. The Federal Reserve buys them with dollars that didn't previously exist. The dollars enter the economy and the debt accumulates on the national balance sheet. I'm describing a mechanism here rather than passing judgement on it.

Nine years ago I wrote about the patterns I was seeing in America, and one of them was a parallel between late Roman currency debasement and modern monetary policy. It felt speculative at the time. It feels considerably less speculative now.

**What Rome Actually Did**

The Roman Empire, in its declining centuries, repeatedly debased its currency to fund expenditures its tax base couldn't support. The denarius, nearly pure silver under Augustus, contained barely five percent silver by the reign of Gallienus.

Nobody did this out of malice or stupidity, and I think that's the important part. They did it because the alternative - genuine reform of the underlying economic structure - was politically impossible. The legions needed paying. The people needed bread. The borders needed defending. The money wasn't there, so the money was made less valuable, and the difference between what it was worth and what the government insisted it was worth became the hidden tax that funded the empire's continuation.

Now watch what's happening. The United States can't fund its current commitments from tax revenue, which was true before the pandemic and is dramatically more true now. The deficit has exploded. The spending is enormous and much of it is genuinely necessary - relief, unemployment support, the basic maintenance of a society in crisis. I want to be clear that I'm not arguing the spending was wrong. It's the mechanism for funding it that has historical parallels worth taking seriously.

When a state can't address structural problems directly, it reaches for monetary manipulation as a substitute for reform. The emperor debased the coin. The central bank prints. Different mechanism, same pattern. The can gets kicked down the road, and the road shortens with every kick.

**Who Actually Pays**

The consequences aren't evenly distributed, and this receives insufficient attention - perhaps because the people who discuss monetary policy professionally are disproportionately among the beneficiaries.

New money enters the economy at the top, flowing first into financial assets. Stocks rise. Property values increase. Bond prices elevate. The people who own these things become wealthier without having created or produced anything, because the denominator changed underneath them. Their assets are priced in dollars, there are now more dollars, so the price goes up.

People who don't own financial assets experience the reverse. Wages don't rise at the rate of asset inflation. Rents climb as property values climb. Savings held in cash lose purchasing power in a currency being quietly diluted.

The money printer is a regressive tax nobody voted for. It transfers wealth from the young to the old, from the assetless to the asset-rich, from the bottom of the distribution to the top, and it does so silently through a mechanism most people don't understand and that is never put to any electorate.

In Australia the Reserve Bank has joined in. The amounts are smaller because the economy is smaller, and the principle is identical. Rates at historic lows. Bond purchases that would have been unthinkable a year ago. The explicit intention of pushing asset prices higher, presented as stimulus and functioning in practice as a further subsidy to asset ownership. House prices here were already disconnected from wages before the pandemic and will be more so afterwards, because the money will find its way into property, because that's where Australian money has always gone, because the tax system and the regulatory settings and the cultural orientation all point the same direction.

**Visible Debasement**

I don't know how this ends, and I'd distrust anyone who claimed to. The Roman pattern suggests it ends badly and slowly - slowly enough that each generation can tell itself things are roughly normal and the system will self-correct. It didn't self-correct in Rome. The debasement continued until the currency stopped functioning as a store of value and the economy reorganised around different foundations.

Whether the modern version follows the same path is genuinely uncertain. Modern economies are vastly more complex. Central banks have instruments no emperor possessed. The capacity for correction exists, at least in theory.

But theory requires political will, political will requires a public that understands what's happening, and the mechanism is specifically designed to be difficult to understand. Quantitative easing. Asset purchase programs. Yield curve control. The language is technical and deliberately so.

That's where I'd intervene, and it's a smaller ask than it sounds. Every central bank should be required to publish, quarterly and in plain language, the distributional consequence of its own actions: how much asset prices moved, who holds those assets by income decile, and what happened to real wages over the same period. One page. No jargon.

I'd start there because the Roman debasement had one honest quality ours lacks entirely - it was visible. You could weigh the coin and see it was lighter. A farmer in Gaul who couldn't read Latin could still feel the difference in his hand. Our version is invisible by construction, buried in policy announcements that almost nobody reads and fewer would parse. A distributional statement doesn't restrain a central bank or bind it to anything. It simply puts the weight of the coin back into people's hands, and lets them decide whether they're content with it.

The money printer goes brrr, as the meme has it, and the joke is funny because it's accurate. The question is who pays, and the answer is the people least equipped to understand the mechanism by which they're paying. The young. The assetless. The ones who sell labour rather than own capital.

The emperor debased the currency because reform was politically impossible. The Fed prints because reform is politically impossible. The pattern rhymes, and whether it resolves the same way remains to be seen. I wouldn't bet against the pattern, and I'd rather we made it visible while we still have the option.
